newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli finance minister Meridor quits.
newsitem.headline: Israeli finance minister Meridor quits.

text.p: Israeli Finance Minister Dan Meridor resigned on Wednesday, losing a power struggle with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu over widening the exchange rate band of the shekel.
"Finance Minister Meridor has resigned," a Treasury spokesman said after ministers at a seven-hour cabinet meeting overwhelmingly rejected his position on the issue.
Meridor strongly opposed widening the shekel's trading bands, fearing it would lead to a further appreciation of the Israeli currency, hurting exports and causing the economy to slow.
Political commentators said the row over how far the shekel should be allowed to fluctuate was the ammunition Netanyahu needed to squeeze his long-time Likud party rival out of the cabinet.
Netanyahu only reluctantly appointed Meridor to be finance chief last year under pressure from party activists.

The prime minister was widely reported to have been angered by what he considered Meridor's lukewarm support in a government corruption scandal over the short-lived appointment of an attorney-general last January.

Political analyst Hanan Crystal said before Meridor quit that Netanyahu might be using economic talks on foreign currency reforms to move on a government shake-up that could give current Infrastructure Minister Ariel Sharon the finance portfolio.
Crystal said such a move would leave young Likud leaders like Meridor who might challenge Netanyahu for party leadership outside the government circle.

Netanyahu had held marathon overnight talks with Meridor and Bank of Israel Governor Jacob Frenkel, and met them again on Wednesday afternoon, in a bid to reach agreement on widening the shekel trading bands.
Frenkel had pushed for expanding the bands, which would give the central bank some relief from the need to constantly intervene in the currency market.
High interest rates have buoyed the shekel, forcing the Bank of Israel to buy massive amounts of dollars to prevent the shekel from strenghtening beyond its band.
The shekel, pegged to a basket of foreign currencies, is allowed to trade in a band of seven percent above or below a diagonal slope desinged to devalue the Israeli currency by six percent a year.
Israeli Army Radio said ministers voted eight to three in favour of Netanyahu's compromise on a shekel fluctuation, but the report did not give precise details about the prime minister's proposal.
